other_side: Zitron argues the AI boom needs revenue, debt and venture funding all to keep growing at once. He says nine AI-linked stocks make up about 46 per cent of the Nasdaq 100, that Amazon has billions of GPUs waiting in warehouses, and that around 80 per cent of the top labs' enterprise revenue comes from loss-making startups. He cites Gartner's prediction that most neoclouds will cease to exist as independent firms by 2030, and reads the stored chips as evidence that supply exceeds demand.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is demand: whether customers will pay enough for AI to cover the infrastructure bill. Both accept as fact that CoreWeave's debt has traded at distressed levels, that Amazon has staged billions of dollars of chips awaiting power, that the labs lean on a few large customers, and that Gartner has predicted widespread neocloud failure. The empirical question is why the chips sit idle; the observable is whether GPU rental prices and neocloud financing hold up over the next two quarters, and what Anthropic's audited results show. The residue is worldview: whether concentration is a bubble signature or an early stage of a real platform shift. For Whittemore to be vindicated, idle chips must prove a power problem and enterprise demand must broaden. For Zitron, rental prices must fall and a neocloud must fail without rescue. Both are polemicists with incentives, Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron certain of a bubble and anti-hype. The signal is that both identify revenue concentration as the key risk. Watch the first audited quarterly numbers.
